caption:
South Korea will inspect the glasses of every student at Thursday's college entrance exam, a test more than 500,000 people sit.
It comes days after the top scorer on the national tax accountant exam admitted he cheated with a hidden camera and AI.
Proctors will also check sleeves, collars and buttons for tiny cameras.

Should smart glasses be banned from every exam?

Follow @neurafeed.ai for daily AI news.

paragraphs.text: South Korea will inspect every pair of glasses worn by students at its national college entrance exam, the College Scholastic Ability Test, which takes place on Thursday, November 19, 2026, according to Reuters. Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin announced the checks at a parliamentary hearing on November 16, as the government responds to a cheating case that involved generative AI.

More than 500,000 students sit the exam, The Telegraph and The Next Web reported. Education authorities said each of the roughly 1,300 test sites will have at least one specially trained supervisor who watches for smart glasses and for small cameras hidden in sleeves, collars or buttons.

The measures follow a confession on November 15 by the top scorer on this year's national tax accountant exam. In a video posted on his lawyer's YouTube channel, the 34-year-old said he photographed exam questions with a miniature camera, sent the images to an AI tool and read the answers on a smartphone. He had answered 159 of 160 questions correctly in the first round and ranked first in both rounds.

He sent a written confession to Seoul police through his lawyer, according to The Next Web, and the finance ministry moved to suspend his qualification. The Telegraph reported that he says he is now helping authorities find other cheaters.

Smart devices were added to the list of banned items in July, Reuters reported, and notices outside exam rooms will warn of criminal penalties. A hotline will connect test centers, local education offices and the ministry's control room, and the ministry plans to consult experts on radio signal detectors for next year's test.

At a Cabinet meeting on November 17, Prime Minister Han Seong-sook said the government would activate an interagency emergency response team, according to Yonhap. Phones must be powered off and handed in, glasses and watches will be inspected, bags will be stored outside exam rooms, Wi-Fi around test sites will be managed more tightly and more proctors will be deployed. Han described a zero tolerance policy toward cheating.

Anyone caught with a smart device will have that year's results voided and will be barred from the following year's test, Reuters reported. The ministry plans to work with parliament to extend that ban to between three and 10 years, and offenders may be reported to police. The minister rejected calls from some lawmakers to postpone the exam.

Deputy Education Minister Choi Eun-ok said it is hard to catch every case of cheating without fully blocking communications, The Telegraph reported. South Korean law bans jamming electronic signals, according to The Next Web.

Smart glasses have appeared in exam rooms before. Test takers wore AI smart glasses on an English test in South Korea in June, The Next Web reported, and Financial News, citing CNN, said a candidate wearing smart glasses was caught at a medical school entrance exam in Taiwan.

The response shows how quickly consumer AI hardware has moved into one of the most guarded rituals in South Korean life. Inspecting glasses by hand can stop the most obvious devices, but cameras small enough to hide in a button are harder to find, which is why officials are already talking about detectors for future years.

The first test of the new rules comes on November 19, when the ministry will learn whether manual inspections and extra proctors are enough, and whether lawmakers move ahead with longer bans for cheaters.
